title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1, preregistration SHA-256 archived) to evaluate whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, compact execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a post‑hoc inferential sensitivity bound tied to the archived contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Automating the translation of operator intent into device configuration promises faster NetOps workflows but creates operational risk when generated changes are misordered, incomplete, or unsafe. The dominant safety pattern advocated in recent literature pairs probabilistic configuration generators (LLMs) with deterministic validators or simulators as floor‑safety nets (generate → verify → repair). Despite architectural proposals and small demonstrations, there is limited preregistered, paired A/B evidence quantifying how tightly bounded guarded pipelines affect first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics.

This study implements a narrowly scoped, preregistered paired experiment that evaluates a minimal guarded pipeline: (a) a single shared LLM candidate per task (single‑shot generation), (b) a frozen deterministic validator performing rule and dependency checks and canonicalization, and (c) at most one automated repair attempt when the validator detects violations. The core research question is: Can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under a controlled paired design? Our contributions are (1) a preregistered confirmatory paired experiment with deterministic seed generation and archival of model outputs and validator/repair traces; (2) confirmatory statistics derived from archived per‑task artifacts showing a near‑ceiling baseline and a single corrected discordance; (3) a concise post‑hoc sensitivity quantification tied directly to the observed contingency counts; and (4) artifact‑grounded recommendations for designing future NetOps confirmatory evaluations.
sections.related_work: Prior surveys and systems work document both promise and risk when applying LLMs to network‑configuration tasks. Recent empirical and system papers show that LLMs can synthesize configuration templates or translate intent into device commands in controlled settings (e.g., intent→configuration demonstrations) while also identifying systematic failure modes—hallucination, misordering, and overconfidence—that threaten operational safety [10.1002/nem.2313]. Architecture and review papers advocate generate→verify→repair patterns and deterministic validators as floor‑safety nets for agentic NetOps workflows; applied demonstrations in adjacent domains (medical QA, code repair) show that verifier‑assisted pipelines and bounded repair loops reduce factual errors and improve grounding [10.36227/techrxiv.176784505.56675782/v1, 10.2139/ssrn.6608518]. Classic network verification work (header‑space and specification‑based checking) provides algorithmic foundations for deterministic validators that check reachability and policy constraints without live execution [10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Our study situates itself at the intersection of these strands by running a preregistered, paired evaluation that uses a deterministic verifier plus a bounded automated repair adapter on LLM outputs and measures first‑pass configuration validity under strict archival.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: The experiment was preregistered (id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) before observing outcomes. Confirmatory hypotheses were: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration explicitly used a planning assumption of baseline pass rate = 0.40 for the power calculation that motivated the sample size and the ≥50% relative reduction target. The preregistration record and associated SHA are archived and referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

Design and sampling semantics: We adopted a paired within‑task design with 300 deterministically generated seeds from the frozen task generator. For each seed the same sampled LLM candidate was reused in both arms (shared_initial_candidate semantics): baseline (single‑shot generation) and guarded (the identical candidate validated and—if invalid—subjected to up to one automated repair attempt). The shared‑candidate choice was preregistered and materially increases within‑pair correlation; this reduces the number of informative discordant pairs available for McNemar inference compared with an independent‑draws design. Planned episodes = 600 (two episodes per seed); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1.

Model, validator, and scoring: The declared model in the execution contract was gpt-5-mini. The frozen deterministic validator/repair adapter (validator id deterministic_netops_validator_v5) implements rule and dependency checks, canonicalizes configurations to normalized ASTs, and produces binary pass/fail scoring together with violation codes used to trigger and steer the preregistered automated repair. Scoring semantics apply a full intent‑constraint validation: an output is scored as a success only when the validator deems required command sequences and dependency constraints satisfied. The experiment treated model/provider failures per the preregistered missingness plan (one retry allowed; primary analysis 'complete_pair_primary' drops only pairs where both calls fail).

Primary estimand and analysis plan: The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistered primary test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05) on paired pass/fail outcomes. As prespecified we also computed the absolute risk difference with a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap seed = 1729). Secondary analyses included exact binomial intervals for repair success and sensitivity checks for missingness and contamination. All analysis code and per‑task artifacts are archived; the execution manifest enumerates the archived items referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

Design rationale and consequential choices: We preregistered the shared_initial_candidate semantics to isolate the validator/repair intervention’s effect on a single generated candidate. This choice reflects an operational use case where a single generated plan is assessed and remediated before deployment. It also reduces variability between arms at the cost of fewer discordant pairs for McNemar inference; we discuss the inferential consequences in Results. The single‑iteration repair budget reflects a conservative operational floor‑guardrail intended as a minimal automated remediation step rather than an unbounded repair loop.
sections.results:
Execution accounting (artifact‑derived): Planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 600, complete pairs analyzed = 300, model_calls_used = 301, repair‑stage invocations = 1. No provider or infrastructure failures occurred under the preregistered retry policy; the run recorded zero failed episodes and no deterministic exclusions for contamination under the registered checks. All per‑task normalized responses, validator decisions, and repair traces were archived in the execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle and were the direct source of the numerical counts reported below.

Primary outcomes (artifact counts): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency counts (guarded vs baseline): n11 = 299 (both success), n10 = 1 (guarded success, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline success), n00 = 0 (both fail). These contingency values are produced directly from the archived paired contingency summary in the analysis artifact bundle and were used for confirmatory inference.

Inferential results (preregistered): Applying the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test to the observed contingency yields p = 1.00. The observed absolute paired difference (guarded minus baseline success rate) = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute paired difference = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Repair outcomes (H2): the single allowed automated repair corrected the single invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1); the Clopper–Pearson 95% CI for 1/1 is [0.025, 1.0], reflecting wide uncertainty given the single observed repair case.

Post‑hoc sensitivity bound from artifact counts: The observed number of discordant pairs is n10 + n01 = 1, which implies a hard limit on the resolvable absolute paired difference equal to 1/300 ≈ 0.00333 under the run's sampling semantics (shared candidate per pair). Thus (a) the maximal possible absolute improvement consistent with the observed discordant total is 1/300; (b) the preregistered target absolute improvement corresponding to the planned ≥50% relative reduction (with planned baseline pass rate = 0.40 → planned absolute improvement ≈ 0.30) would require an observed net discordant difference of approximately 0.30×300 = 90 discordant pairs in favor of guarded outputs. In short, the empirical baseline prevalence (299/300) produced effectively no statistical headroom for the preregistered effect size and thereby invalidated the original power planning assumptions.

Representative diagnostic artifacts: Validator traces for each episode include normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, and repair_applied flags. The single baseline failure was corrected by invoking the preregistered repair adapter on the shared candidate; the post‑repair normalized_configuration satisfied the full intent constraints as adjudicated by the deterministic validator. Readers can inspect per‑task validator decisions and repair traces in the archived execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle listed in the Disclosure Statement.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and operational implications: The guarded pipeline corrected the lone invalid baseline output, demonstrating that a frozen deterministic validator plus a bounded automated repair iteration can remediate validator‑detected violations in at least some cases. However, the run does not provide confirmatory support for the preregistered large relative effect (≥50%) because the empirical baseline pass rate was far higher than assumed. Two practical lessons follow.

Difficulty calibration and preregistration targets: Confirmatory NetOps experiments that use paired McNemar inference must anticipate not only sample size but also the expected number of informative discordant pairs. When baseline pass rates are uncertain, we recommend preregistering a target initial‑failure count (not only N) and calibrating the task bank so that the expected number of discordant pairs provides power to detect the targeted absolute effect. Options for calibration include raising task difficulty, adversarially augmenting tasks to induce more failures, or focusing the primary estimand on conditional quantities (e.g., repair effectiveness conditional on initial failure) where the experimented event rate is better controlled.

Pairing semantics, repair budget, and operational realism: The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics reduce cross‑arm variance but also decrease discordance potential; independent draws per arm increase discordance and thus statistical information but impose cross‑arm heterogeneity. The single‑iteration repair budget is a conservative floor‑guardrail; production guardrails commonly permit more repair attempts or human review before deployment. Future confirmatory designs should align pairing semantics and repair budgets with the specific operational claim being evaluated and preregister explicit targets for informative discordant pairs.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is limited by the preregistered choice to reuse the same initial candidate per pair (shared_initial_candidate), which increases within‑pair correlation. Construct validity is limited because the deterministic validator checks canonicalized configuration constraints rather than executing configurations in a live network; runtime packet‑level reachability and performance effects were not measured. External validity is limited by the synthetic task bank, constrained vendor‑template space, a single model family (gpt-5-mini), and a single validator implementation. Conclusion validity is constrained by the small number of informative discordant pairs (one), which leaves confirmatory inference about large preregistered effects unsupported. All these limitations are enumerated in the manuscript limitations section and are reflected in the archived artifacts.

Recommendations for future confirmatory NetOps evaluations: (1) preregister and calibrate task banks to achieve a targeted initial‑failure prevalence (or target discordant‑pair counts) matching the planned inferential effect size; (2) explicitly preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets and include their impact on expected discordant counts in the power plan; (3) when operational claims require runtime assurances, incorporate emulation or simulation steps that exercise packet‑level or control‑plane consequences rather than relying exclusively on static configuration validators; (4) when repair effectiveness is a key operational claim, treat repair success as a conditional estimand (conditional on initial failure) and power the study for sufficient failure counts to estimate that conditional probability precisely.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) using a frozen deterministic validator and a one‑iteration automated repair budget applied to gpt-5-mini outputs, baseline single‑shot generation produced 299/300 valid outputs and the guarded pipeline produced 300/300 valid outputs. The single automated repair corrected the only observed invalid baseline output, but the run does not support the preregistered claim of ≥50% relative reduction in misconfiguration because the observed baseline contradicted the planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) and left no statistical headroom. Future confirmatory NetOps evaluations should (a) calibrate task difficulty to produce sufficient initial failures, (b) preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets explicitly, and (c) measure runtime semantic effects via emulation when operational claims are intended. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, the execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived with the run and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement to permit reproduction of the reported counts and intervals.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.
The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicts that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
